scenes.heading: The Race Detector
scenes.narration: In the next minute, let's understand Go's race detector and how it catches the most dangerous class of concurrency bug.

scenes.heading: What it actually finds
items: Two goroutines touch the same memory
At least one access is a write
scenes.narration: A data race is a precise, mechanical fault: two goroutines access the same memory location, at least one of them writes, and there is no happens-before ordering to sequence them. That is exactly what the detector flags. It does not chase logical race conditions or deadlocks, so knowing this boundary tells you what a green run really proves.

scenes.heading: How ThreadSanitizer works
steps: Track a vector clock per goroutine
Stamp shadow memory on each access
scenes.narration: Building with the race flag makes the compiler inject a hook before every memory read and write and links Google's ThreadSanitizer. Each goroutine carries a vector clock, and synchronization events like channel operations and mutex locks advance and merge those clocks. On every access, the runtime stamps shadow memory, and when it finds two conflicting accesses whose clocks are unordered, it prints a data-race warning with both stack traces.

scenes.heading: An unguarded counter
scenes.narration: Here two goroutines increment the same variable with no synchronization. Because counter plus plus is a read-modify-write, increments get lost and the final value is non-deterministic. Run this normally and it looks fine; run it with go run dash race and the detector prints a data-race warning pointing at this exact line, then exits with status sixty-six.

scenes.text: No false positives, but only sees the interleavings you actually run — so fix every report and stress-test in CI.
scenes.narration: Trust every report, because ThreadSanitizer has no false positives. But it is dynamic, so it only catches races on paths you actually execute. Run go test dash race in CI, add concurrency stress tests, and never suppress a warning — fix the synchronization instead.
